studyPages.title: Cells as Units of Life
studyPages.body:
CELLS AS UNITS OF LIFE
====

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
----
• Say what cells as units of life means in plain words.
• Use one real Kenyan example to show cells as units of life.
• Correct one common mistake about cells as units of life.

INTRODUCTION
----
Every plant leaf and every bit of your skin is built from tiny living units called cells. You cannot see most of them without a microscope, yet they carry out the processes that keep organisms alive. This page starts the cell story from that simple idea.

MAIN NOTES
----
• Cells make up the structure of living organisms and carry out various biological processes.
• Organisms such as amoeba are composed of a single cell hence are said to be unicellular.
• Organisms such as plants and animals are composed of many cells hence are said to be multicellular.
• Therefore, a cell is defined as the basic unit of structure and functions in organisms.
• To observe the cell, a powerful magnifying instrument called a microscope is used.
• Plant and animal cell structures as seen under a light microscope.
• The following diagram shows the components of a plant cell as seen under a light microscope.

WORKED EXAMPLE
----
Worked situation (a hardware shop in Nakuru): a learner investigates cells as units of life. First observation: Cells make up the structure of living organisms and carry out various biological processes. Because of that observation, the learner names the correct scientific idea and rejects a near-miss confusion. So the conclusion is written in one accurate sentence that matches the main notes — with the correct symbol or formula if one applies (H₂O, NaCl, Fe, P = F / A).

IN EVERYDAY LIFE
----
At a hardware shop in Nakuru, cells as units of life shows up when you handle real materials or processes linked to this idea. Safety tip: if you see smoke, raise the alarm early and do not fight a large fire alone.

SUMMARY
----
• Cells make up the structure of living organisms and carry out various biological processes.
• Organisms such as amoeba are composed of a single cell hence are said to be unicellular.
• Organisms such as plants and animals are composed of many cells hence are said to be multicellular.
• Therefore, a cell is defined as the basic unit of structure and functions in organisms.

REVISION QUESTIONS
----
1. Define cells as units of life in your own words and give one clear example.
2. Describe a situation at a hardware shop in Nakuru that shows cells as units of life, and explain the science involved.
3. A learner makes a mistake about cells as units of life. State a likely wrong idea, correct it, and justify your correction with facts from this page.

ANSWERS
----
1. Cells make up the structure of living organisms and carry out various biological processes. For example, link it to a real object or event at home, school, market or shamba that fits this page.
2. At a hardware shop in Nakuru, you would observe something that matches cells as units of life. Name the observation, then explain it using the definition above. End by stating why the correct idea matters for accuracy or safety.
3. Wrong idea: confusing cells as units of life with a neighbouring concept or ignoring a key rule. Correct idea: Cell theory intro for Grade 8. Justification: the worked example on this page shows the right reasoning with real objects or numbers.

The science under it is Eyepiece objective stage mirror/lamp. That is the whole job of this page: name it correctly and apply it.

MAIN NOTES
----
• A microscope enlarges the image of objects when observed and improves the resolution of the image.
• The figures below show the components of both plant and animal cells as seen under a light microscope.
• Magnification of a specimen is the measure of how much bigger a specimen is when it is viewed through a hand lens or microscope compared to its original size.
• It is a measure of how much bigger an object appears when viewed through a hand lens or microscope, for example X2 means the object has been magnified or enlarged two times or the image is twice bigger than the actual object.
• For a light microscope, the final magnified image of an object as seen by the observer is the product of the magnifying power of the lenses that are used. These lenses include eyepiece lens and the objective lens.
• The magnifying power of each of these lenses is marked on the sides of the objective and eye piece lens holder.
• In a light microscope, the revolving nosepiece holds three different objective lenses, each with a specific magnifying power of X4, X10 and X40. The eyepiece lens further magnifies the image formed by the objective lens.

====

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
----
• Say what plant cell structures means in plain words.
• Use one real Kenyan example to show plant cell structures.
• Correct one common mistake about plant cell structures.

INTRODUCTION
----
An onion epidermis under the microscope shows box-like cells with walls — a clue you are looking at plant cells. Plant cells typically show a cell wall, membrane, nucleus, cytoplasm, vacuole and, in green parts, chloroplasts.

MAIN NOTES
----
• Cell wall helps the cell to keep its shape.
• It is an organelle in the cytoplasm of plant cells. Chloroplast contain green pigment called chlorophyll.
• Both have nucleus within them.
• It acts like a fence and controls what goes in and out of the cell.
• Therefore, the cell can take in substances it needs and get rid of waste products.
• It is a jelly-like liquid that fills inside the cell.
• The cytoplasm is where chemical reactions of the cell take place.

----
• Both have nucleus within them.
• The nucleus carries genetic information and controls what happens or all the activities of the cell.
• It also contains small structures called organelles.

MAIN NOTES
----
• A light microscope uses more than one lens to enlarge a specimen.
• Total magnification = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification.
• If the eyepiece is ×10 and the objective is ×40, total magnification is ×400. That means the image looks four hundred times larger than the real specimen.

WORKED EXAMPLE
----
Faith uses an eyepiece marked ×10 and an objective marked ×40.

Working:
1. Formula / relationship: Total magnification = eyepiece × objective
2. Substitute values: Total = 10 × 40
3. Total = 400
Final Answer: ×400
Mark reminder: method mark for multiplying lens powers; accuracy mark for × value

Brian wrongly adds 10 + 40 = 50. That is incorrect because total magnification multiplies the lens powers. First write the formula, then substitute, then multiply — never add the markings.

sources.excerpt: 2.1 The Cell. Cells make up the structure of living organisms and carry out various biological processes. Organisms such as amoeba are composed of a single cell hence are said to be unicellular.
